extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional screenwriters; students of dramatic writing
extracted.subtask_description: A blog-post reading list that summarizes classic screenwriting/playwriting books and extracts concrete screenwriting principles (character, premise, conflict, structure, and the author's 'Hero Goal Sequence' system) for writers to study and apply. Includes recommended titles and practical rules-of-thumb for constructing sympathetic heroes and sequence counts for commercial one-hero American movies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as the foundation that drives plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Egri argues against Aristotle's claim that plot is primary, asserting that well-defined characters can drive the plot themselves and that 'good dramatic writing hinges on people and their relationships.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize character definition, motivations and relationships as the engine of story. Egri devotes nearly 100 pages to character and then treats conflict, foreshadowing, transitions, exposition, character entrances/exits and dialogue. Use characters' actions (not mere description) to reveal who they are; treat character development and motivation as central to constructing drama. Examples cited: Shakespeare, Ibsen. (Original phrasing: 'well-defined characters can drive the plot themselves... good dramatic writing hinges on people and their relationships.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a clear thesis / premise to guide dramatic conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The author must have a thesis (premise) and develop dramatic conflict around that thesis/theme so the writer knows where the story is going.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State a central premise (Egri example: 'stinginess leads to ruin') and use it to fashion beginning, middle and end. Structure scenes to first establish a trait (e.g., stinginess), then present opposition, then show how the trait leads to ruin or change (or redemption). The premise guides what must happen and why. (Original phrasing: 'Without the thesis, or premise, how can one know where a story is going, Egri asks?')

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conflict and foreshadowing; make change central to drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict and the foreshadowing of conflict are core dramatic tools; change (characters evolving/synthesizing new philosophies under pressure) is ever-present in life and drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build conflict into character arcs and plot beats; foreshadow future confrontations. Treat change as the engine that forces evolution in characters when facing overwhelming obstacles. Chapters in classic texts emphasize using conflict and foreshadowing strategically to generate drama and forward motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dramatic irony and tragic-flaw structure (classical tragedy techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophocles' Oedipus Rex demonstrates how dramatic irony and a central character flaw (hubris) contribute to a tragic hero's downfall; classical tragic structures remain a blueprint for modern screenwriters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ dramatic irony and revealable flaws so audience knowledge heightens emotional impact. Center theme around a fatal flaw (e.g., hubris) that precipitates catastrophe; use recognition and reversal as powerful structural devices. (Original phrasing: 'It contains an emphasis on how the central character's own inner flaw of hubris contributes to this tragic hero's downfall.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Aristotle's Poetics principles to dramatic construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's elements—plot, character, language and spectacle—and concepts such as mimesis, hamartia and catharsis remain central: effective tragedies rely on complication & resolution, recognition & reversals, and centering on heroic characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Aristotle's framework to create pity and fear in audiences: aim for tightly constructed complications and resolutions, meaningful recognitions and reversals, and properly scaled heroic characters. Adapt these classical concepts to modern screen narratives rather than copying ancient forms verbatim. (Original phrasing: 'Aristotle examines the dramatic elements of plot, character, language and spectacle... introduced such hero development concepts as mimesis (imitation), hamartia (error), and catharsis, or purification.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and synthesize historical and contemporary dramatic elements (Lance Lee's overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lance Lee offers a historical perspective and an overview of dramatic elements without bias toward any single screenwriting method, covering primary plot elements, dramatic reality, storytelling stance, plot types, character, mind in drama, spectacle, and developing/filming the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the evolution of dramaturgy and adapt classical ideas (Aristotle, Greek tragedy, Shakespeare, Ibsen) to modern film practice. Consider plot types, audience 'dramatic reality,' storytelling stance, and practical production considerations (developing and filming) when shaping a screenplay. Use examples from classic and contemporary films to illustrate principles. (Original phrasing: 'a thorough overview of all the dramatic elements of screenplays without displaying a specific bias toward any one particular screenwriting method.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Write visually—use the tools of visual dramatic storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: When converting treatments or books to screenplays, rely on the tools of visual dramatic storytelling rather than expository or purely literary devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show story through action, images, and behavior rather than through exposition. Emphasize 'live visual dramatic storytelling'—what can be seen and heard on screen—when shaping scenes, transitions, and character revelations. The post stresses training in story-building craft specifically for visual mediums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero Goal Sequence: definition and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: A Goal Sequence is a 2–8 page screenplay segment in which the hero pursues a single short-term physical goal; it ends when the hero discovers FRESH NEWS that creates a new short-term goal and begins the next sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Goal Sequences as the primary outlining tool. Each sequence (2–8 pages) should contain a clear short-term objective and conclude with 'FRESH NEWS' that changes the hero's immediate goal. This modular approach is presented as the 'strongest outlining tool' for building scripts and novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero Goal Sequence counts and placement rules for commercial one-hero American movies
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercially successful one-hero American movies contain between 20 and 23 Hero Goal Sequences, arranged across three acts with specific landmark placements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the prescribed sequence counts and landmark placements: Act One ALWAYS contains six Hero Goal Sequences and Stunning Surprise One ALWAYS takes place as FRESH NEWS in sequence #6. Act Two ALWAYS contains 12 more Hero Goal Sequences, with the Midpoint Sequence ALWAYS occurring during Hero Goal Sequence #12. Stunning Surprise Two ALWAYS arrives as FRESH NEWS in Sequence #18. Act Three contains a minimum of two and a maximum of five Hero Goal Sequences. These are presented as firm guiding rules in 'The Story Solution.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a sympathetic lead by balancing flaws with strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a lead character we care about does not mean inventing a flawless person; heroes should be eccentric or defensive at times, but their strengths must outnumber their failings for emotional connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance character flaws with overriding strengths so readers/audiences can empathize. Avoid perfect protagonists; give them quirks and mistakes, but ensure strengths dominate. Use Goal Sequences to expose both strengths and flaws through action rather than telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personality traits and plot circumstances that create sympathetic heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-exhaustive list of traits and circumstances that help create sympathetic heroes: Courage; Unfair Injury (creates imperative to act); Skill; Funny; Nice; In Danger; Loved by Friends and Family; Hard Working; Obsessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider incorporating one or more of these traits/circumstances to increase audience sympathy and engagement. 'Unfair Injury' should demand that the hero DO something in response; 'Obsessed' and 'Hard Working' create forward momentum; being 'Loved' gives immediate permission for audiences to care. Use these elements in combination to craft a well-rounded, relatable protagonist.
